chunks: "A CPU is designed to make one thread run as fast as possible, and a GPU is designed to finish as much total work per second as possible. That one decision drives everything else.
A CPU spends its transistors on a few big cores with out-of-order execution, branch predictors and large caches, because it needs to cope with branchy, irregular code and keep latency low.
A GPU spends them on thousands of simple ALU lanes, huge register files and wide memory interfaces. Its threads are slower individually, but there are tens of thousands of them.
They hide memory latency differently too. A CPU uses big caches and speculation to avoid stalling.
A GPU just switches to another warp when one stalls, so it needs lots of parallel work. A GPU also executes threads in lockstep groups, so divergent branches hurt.

The result is that CPUs win on serial, control-heavy, latency-sensitive code like operating systems and most application logic, while GPUs win on regular data-parallel work like graphics, matrix multiplication and image processing, often by 10 to 100 times.
In a real system they're partners: the CPU runs the control flow and ships the heavy parallel kernels to the GPU, as long as the data transfer cost doesn't eat the gain."
